summary: 1. Lead hooks with extreme contrast or high-stakes survival (e.g., a thin sheet saving astronauts' lives reached 59.4% stayed) instead of academic curiosity. 2. Never reveal list items or answers in sentence one; listing the smoke detector and watch immediately dropped retention to 6.7%. 3. Replace passive rhetorical questions like 'Ever thought why...' with active mystery framing, as weak rhetorical intros bottomed out at 11.1% stayed. 4. Maintain a 42-45 second video length; cutting under 35 seconds correlated with lowest views (9) and instant swiping. 5. Write curiosity-gap titles ending with '🤯' and active problem-solving phrasing ('कैसे बचता है', 'Will Insulate') rather than flat descriptive labels.
winning_hooks: High-stakes paradox: 'Space missions mein astronauts ke liye sirf ek thin plastic sheet jaan bacha sakti hai 🤯' (59.4% stayed)
High-velocity concrete dilemma: '250 km/h की speed से गीली runway पर plane hydroplaning से कैसे बचता है?' (Highest views: 72)
Bizarre physical discovery: 'डायनासोर के जीवाश्मों में वैज्ञानिकों को ऐसी सूक्ष्म आकृतियां क्यों मिली हैं...' (37.0% stayed)
avoid: Lazy rhetorical prompts like 'Ever thought why...' (produced lowest view count: 9 views, 11.1% stayed)
Immediate payoff spoilers that list the examples in the hook (e.g., naming smoke detectors and vintage watches upfront sank stayed rate to 6.7%)
Textbook encyclopedic titles without stakes (e.g., 'How Deep Ocean Snow Moves Carbon' or 'Common Household Items That Contain Radioactive Materials')
Sub-35 second durations that lack sufficient narrative build-up before the drop-off
next_experiment: A/B test the Radioactive Items video hook: Arm A tests the original spoiler hook ('Kuch everyday objects secretly radioactive hote hain jaise watch aur smoke detector'), Arm B tests a blind curiosity gap ('Aapke bedroom mein rakhi ek aam cheez subtle radiation emit kar rahi hai, aur aapko pata bhi nahi'). Measure if hiding the item name triples stayed_pct above 50%.
